query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A dual‐phase high–entropy alloy, specifically an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, will show markedly superior resistance to combined high-temperature corrosion and mechanical wear (tribo‐corrosion) compared to conventional alloys because its engineered microstructure forms a protective and noble-element–enriched surface layer that slows selective phase dissolution.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high–entropy alloy with a lamellar microstructure comprising an FCC phase (acting as a barrier) and a B2 phase susceptible to selective dissolution.
generation.intervention: Exposure to high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions, for example in a molten salt environment (e.g., NaCl–KCl–MgCl2) at temperatures around 450°C to 650°C under sliding wear loads.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under controlled high-temperature molten salt conditions combined with mechanical sliding/wear to simulate tribo-corrosive degradation in extreme environments (such as in concentrating solar power or similar applications).
generation.structural_mediator: The dual-phase (FCC + B2) microstructure that leads to micro-galvanic coupling and the formation of a protective, noble-element–enriched surface layer that limits further oxidation and elemental dissolution.
generation.mechanism: Selective dissolution of the more reactive phase (B2) and galvanic coupling between phases promote the enrichment of more oxidation-resistant elements in the protective FCC matrix. This effect reduces both chemical corrosion and mechanical material removal during tribo-corrosion, thereby slowing overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The EHEA should exhibit a significantly lower combined corrosion and wear (tribo-corrosion) rate compared with conventional alloys (e.g., duplex stainless steels such as DS2205), with a reduction expected on the order of approximately 50% or more under comparable conditions, though the exact quantitative difference remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: Performance of conventional alloys (such as DS2205 duplex stainless steel) under similar high-temperature, corrosive, and tribological conditions.
generation.boundary: The improved performance is expected within the tested temperature range (approximately 450°C to 650°C) and under molten salt conditions similar to those used in concentrating solar power applications; behavior at significantly higher temperatures or in different corrosive environments may deviate.
generation.uncertainty: While reduced corrosion rates in molten salt have been observed for this alloy, its behavior under dynamic tribological (wear) conditions remains less well quantified; further tests are needed to determine exact performance improvements under various tribo-corrosion stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA and a conventional duplex stainless steel such as DS2205. Subject both material types to a combined high-temperature tribo-corrosion test in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at 450°C and 650°C under controlled sliding wear conditions (using, for example, a tribometer in a heated chamber). Monitor mass loss, wear track profile, and surface chemistry alterations over a fixed test duration.
measurements: Wear track analysis via microscopy (profilometry, SEM)
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., EDS and Kelvin probe mapping) to assess protective layer formation
Comparative measurement of mechanical properties pre- and post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA does not show a significant reduction (e.g., at least 50% lower combined tribo-corrosion degradation) compared to DS2205 under identical test conditions, or if no protective phase enrichment is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
